prompt: Capacity dispute for a worker service, need a tiebreaker. The service pulls jobs off a queue with a fixed pool of 4 worker threads, one job per thread at a time. Our SRE's sizing note says: "p50 job time is 40ms; 60 jobs/s x 0.04s = 2.4 busy workers, so a pool of 4 gives us ~40% headroom." But in practice, every time peak traffic hits, queue depth climbs steadily for as long as peak lasts and only drains after traffic drops — which shouldn't happen with 40% headroom. Product wants to know if bumping the pool to 6 fixes it. Using the numbers above: how many busy workers does this workload actually demand at 60 jobs/s, is the SRE's headroom math right, and what's the minimum pool size that keeps the queue from growing at peak (with sensible margin)?
hidden_trap: Offered load must use the MEAN service time, not the median. Mean = 0.95x0.04 + 0.05x2.5 = 0.038 + 0.125 = 0.163s, so demand = 60 x 0.163 = 9.78 busy workers. The rare 2.5s jobs carry most of the load (0.125 of the 0.163). A pool of 4 runs at ~245% utilization — hence the unbounded queue growth — and 6 is still ~163% utilized and also diverges. Minimum stable pool is 10 (utilization ~98%, still queue-heavy), so a sensible answer is ~12-13 for real headroom. Tempting wrong: bless the p50-based 2.4-worker math or approve the bump to 6.

prompt: Planning a maintenance window and my teammate's estimate feels off but I can't articulate why. Our session cache is sharded across memcached nodes with plain modulo: node = hash(user_id) % NUM_SHARDS, hash is effectively uniform. We're expanding NUM_SHARDS from 10 to 12 this Saturday. Teammate's capacity note: "We're adding 2 shards out of 12, so roughly 2/12 ≈ 17% of keys will land on a different node after the change. Cold-start impact: ~17% cache miss spike, well within what the DB can absorb, so no need for a warmup phase — 30-minute window is plenty." The DB headroom math downstream of that 17% is fine, I checked it. But the 17% itself — is that actually what fraction of keys move when you go from mod 10 to mod 12? Can you work out the real fraction, and tell me whether skipping the warmup phase is still defensible?
hidden_trap: With modulo sharding almost everything moves. A key stays iff hash % 10 == hash % 12, which for uniform hashes happens iff (hash mod 60) is in {0..9} — exactly 10 of 60 residues — so only 1/6 ≈ 16.7% of keys STAY and ~83.3% move. The teammate's 17% is (coincidentally) the fraction that stays, not the fraction that moves; the intuition '2 new shards ≈ 2/12 moved' describes consistent hashing, not modulo. A ~83% miss spike invalidates the no-warmup plan; the answer should recommend warmup/gradual migration or consistent hashing. Tempting wrong: confirm ~17% move, or hand-wave 'most keys remap' without deriving the 1/6 stay fraction.

States ~83% of keys move, directly contradicting the 17%-move estimate
Notes the 2/12 intuition is a consistent-hashing property that modulo sharding does not have
Concludes the no-warmup 30-minute plan is not defensible at an ~83% miss spike (recommends warmup, staged migration, or consistent hashing)

prompt: Release go/no-go call in an hour, need a gut check on our canary evidence. We're rolling out a rewritten checkout endpoint. The SLO for the new endpoint is an error rate below 1%. The canary plan sent 20 production requests through the new code path; all 20 succeeded, zero errors. The release manager's summary reads: "Canary observed 0% error rate over 20 requests. 0% < 1%, SLO demonstrated, cleared for 100% rollout." Something about concluding a sub-1% error rate from 20 samples bothers me, but I can't put numbers on it and 'the sample point estimate is inside the SLO' is technically true. Two questions: (a) if the new endpoint actually had, say, a 5% or 10% error rate — clear SLO violations — how likely is it that this exact canary (20/20 clean) would still have passed? (b) roughly how many consecutive error-free canary requests would we need before 20/20-style evidence actually supports 'error rate < 1%' at something like 95% confidence?
hidden_trap: Zero-failures-in-n gives weak evidence for small n. (a) A true 5% error rate passes 20/20 clean with probability 0.95^20 ≈ 35.8%; a true 10% rate passes with 0.9^20 ≈ 12.2% — so this canary would frequently green-light clear SLO violations. (b) To claim error rate < 1% at 95% confidence with zero observed errors you need 0.99^n ≤ 0.05, i.e. n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.99) ≈ 298 → about 300 error-free requests (rule of three: 95% upper bound ≈ 3/n, so 20 requests only bounds the rate at ~15%). Tempting wrong: agree 0/20 demonstrates the SLO, or give confidence-interval hand-waving without the 0.95^20 and ~300 numbers.
pass_criteria: Answers (a) with 0.95^20 ≈ 36% and/or 0.9^20 ≈ 12%, showing the canary passes badly-broken builds a large fraction of the time
Answers (b) with roughly 300 error-free requests (accept 250-350, or the rule-of-three 3/0.01=300 formulation), noting 20 requests only bounds the error rate near 14-15%
Concludes the release manager's 'SLO demonstrated' claim is unsupported, distinguishing the point estimate from a confidence bound
fail_tells: Accepts 0/20 as demonstrating the sub-1% SLO
Discusses sample-size concerns qualitatively but provides neither the ~36%/12% pass probabilities nor the ~300-request figure
Produces a wildly wrong n (e.g. claims a few dozen samples suffice, or demands tens of thousands with faulty math)
